question: Who is speaking at the end of a cycle about childhood?
intro: The cycle ends with the grown-up looking back. Chords in G major move together, a loosened passage of single lines and fermatas interrupts them, and the chords return and slow to a held chord.

sections.label: C · single lines and held notes
sections.mNote: grace figures, triplets, fermatas in the high register

sections.label: A′ · the chords return and slow
sections.mNote: opening chords again, ending on a held chord

cues.title: Chords that move together
cues.text: Common time in G major, marked p with a swelling hairpin. Both hands play chords that move as a block, with the pedal down, so the writing sounds like a hymn heard slowly. The attacks are sparse, at most about 1.4 a second in the first twenty seconds.
cues.evidence: First edition p. 20 (IMSLP #03060): common time, one sharp, p with hairpin, chords in both hands, Ped. Report: G major at 0:00–0:20, 0.4–1.4 onsets per second, −19.4 dB at 0:00 rising to −16.6 dB at 0:10.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The quietest stretch so far
cues.text: Marked pp, the next chords fall away: the report’s relative level drops to about −33 dB between 0:25 and 0:35, the lowest in the first minute. The loud return at 0:40 is by contrast a sudden step up.
cues.evidence: Report: −32.6 dB at 0:25, −29.5 dB at 0:30, −34.3 dB at 0:35, then −13.0 dB at 0:40 (listed among the loudest windows); novelty 0.36 at 0:36 and 0.41 at 0:40. Score p. 20, second system: pp over two bars, then p.

cues.title: Descending lines, two fermatas
cues.text: The chords give way to descending lines marked p, with ritardando and two fermatas over the melody. In the recording the rate of attacks sinks to 0.6 a second and the level to −31 dB near 0:55, the first long pause.
cues.evidence: Report: novelty 0.41 at 0:40 and 0.32 at 0:58; −31.0 dB and 0.6 onsets per second at 0:55. Score p. 20, second system: p, descending lines, rit., two fermatas above the staff.

cues.title: The barlines disappear
cues.text: From about 1:00 a free, recitative-like passage of single lines replaces the chords: grace figures, triplet groups, fermatas and many chromatic notes, mostly in the right hand’s high register. The report’s brightness rises from about 500 Hz to between 714 and 879 Hz.
cues.evidence: Report: spectral centroid 609 Hz at 0:55 and 872, 856, 714, 879 Hz at 1:00, 1:05, 1:10, 1:15, against about 500 Hz elsewhere. Local key estimates in this span (E♭ minor 0.36, B major 0.55, C♯ minor 0.53–0.67) are low-confidence and are not used as harmony. Score p. 20, third system: no barlines, fermatas, “3” groups, grace figures, pp, rit.

cues.title: Twelve chosen, thirteen printed
cues.text: In March 1838 Schumann told Clara he had picked “about twelve” from some thirty pieces. The printed set has thirteen, and this one closes it. In 1956 Ludwig Kusche used the title Der Dichter spricht for a collection of Schumann’s own writings.
cues.evidence: Zwickau catalogue 175 Jahre Kinderszenen, item 3 (letter begun 17 March 1838: “von denen ich etwa zwölf ausgelesen”) and item 35 (Kusche, Der Dichter spricht, Munich 1956).

cues.title: The chords come back
cues.text: Near 1:24 the opening chords return. The report’s strongest boundary falls here, and the form analysis finds the opening 22 seconds heard again at 1:26–1:48.
cues.evidence: Report: novelty 1.00 at 1:24; −31.7 dB at 1:20 then −21.3 dB at 1:25 with G major at 1:30–1:35. Form analysis: 0:02.5–0:24 matches 1:26.5–1:48 (lag 84 s, mean 0.95, contrast 0.52).

cues.title: Slowing onto a held chord
cues.text: The last system is marked ritardando over long hairpins and ends on a held chord with a fermata. The relative level sinks from −28 dB at 2:25 to −41 dB at 2:30 and −55 dB at 2:35; the final chord dies away by about 2:40.
cues.evidence: Report: −28.3 dB at 2:25, −40.5 dB at 2:30, −54.9 dB at 2:35, −73.4 dB at 2:40; novelty 0.47 at 2:26 and 0.55 at 2:30. Score p. 20, last system: rit., dan, do, hairpins, fermata over the final chord.

transitions.title: Chords yield to descending lines
transitions.how: The pp chords that opened the second phrase give way to a p passage of single descending lines, with a ritardando and two fermatas over the melody. The block of chords loosens into separate voices, and the music begins to pause on single notes instead of moving on.
transitions.evidence: Report: −34.3 dB at 0:35, −13.0 dB at 0:40, novelty 0.41 at 0:40; −31.0 dB and 0.6 onsets per second at 0:55. Score p. 20, second system: pp then p, rit. and two fermatas.

transitions.title: Fermatas and single lines in the treble
transitions.to: C · single lines and held notes
transitions.how: After the ritardando and fermatas the score abandons barlines. Single lines move freely, like recitative, with grace figures, triplet groups and fermatas at several points. The line climbs into the treble through chromatic notes, so the block chords of the opening give way to the least chord-like writing in the piece.
transitions.evidence: Report: novelty 0.32 at 0:58; spectral centroid 609 Hz at 0:55 and 872 Hz at 1:00. Score p. 20, third system: no barlines; fermatas, triplet groups and grace figures in the right hand.

transitions.title: A fermata, then the chords return
transitions.from: C · single lines and held notes
transitions.to: A′ · the chords return and slow
transitions.how: The single lines end with a ritardando and a fermata, and the opening chords come back, marked p with a hairpin as at the start. Barlines and the block chords return with the G-major writing of the first system, so the free passage reads as an interruption.
transitions.evidence: Report: −31.7 dB at 1:20, novelty 1.00 at 1:24, G major at 1:30–1:35. Form analysis: the opening 0:02.5–0:24 returns at 1:26.5–1:48 (mean 0.95). Score p. 20, third to fourth systems: rit. and fermata, then p and the opening chords.

composer.epithet: His music lets remembered fragments, concealed names and competing inner voices interrupt the forms that contain them.
facts: Piano with Friedrich Wieck; composition with Heinrich Dorn; extensive private study of Bach and Beethoven
Co-founder of the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik, 1834; editor until 1844
Married Clara Wieck in 1840; eight children, seven surviving infancy
Leipzig Conservatoire teacher; municipal music director, Düsseldorf, 1850–53
composer.background:
Schumann grew up in Zwickau, where his father August was a bookseller and publisher. Reading and music developed together: Jean Paul’s novels, with their interruptions, doubles and changes of narrative voice, mattered alongside piano lessons. Sent to Leipzig to study law in 1828, he spent more time on music and literature; a period in Heidelberg did not reconcile him to a legal career. He returned to Leipzig to study piano seriously with Friedrich Wieck. Wieck’s daughter Clara, already performing publicly as a child, gave him an immediate example of the professional discipline he hoped to acquire.

A persistent problem with his right hand ended the prospect of a virtuoso career. The familiar account of a finger-strengthening device leaves the injury’s medical cause uncertain. Composition and criticism became his principal occupations. The early published piano works already had distinct literary and formal premises: the Abegg Variations derive a theme from letters, while Papillons relates its dances to the masked-ball ending of Jean Paul’s Flegeljahre. The miniatures’ sudden juxtapositions recreate the experience of a narrative changing speakers and levels.
